name: Question 1
problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $6{x}^{3}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ which differential equation describes this motion?
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14097535/assets/52fc197612dac35373ecebf771b8444505902b5c6e00c7c55d2b21dab4809136.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $6{x}^{3}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6{x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-6{x}^{3}.
$$

Question 1
?

A particle P moves along the x-axis where x>0. When the displacement of P from the origin O is x meters, its velocity is vm/s and the magnitude of its acceleration is 6x3m/s2. Given that the acceleration is directed toward O, which differential equation describes this motion?

a
dvdx=−6x3
b
dvdx=6x3
c
ddx(12v2)=6x3
d
ddx(12v2)=−6x3
e
ddx(v2)=−6x3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since the acceleration of the particle P has magnitude 6x3 and is directed toward O, we have dvdt=−6x3.

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as dvdx⋅dxdt=−6x3.

Now, since v=dxdt, we have vdvdx=6x3.(∗)

Finally, using the fact that

ddx(v2)=2vdvdx⟹ddx(12v2)=vdvdx,

we can write our differential equation (∗) as

ddx(12v2)=−6x3.
